subject: Data Structure
verificationNote: Answers written against paper ID 311623; tree and addressing/hash calculations independently simulated. Some code questions use function-level C algorithms rather than standalone compilable full programs and should be expanded for a complete exam-length model answer.

questions.question: Why are pointers required to maintain a linked-list structure?
questions.answer: A linked-list node stores data and an address/reference to another node. The pointer (next, and sometimes prev) connects separately allocated nodes without requiring contiguous memory, enabling dynamic insertion, deletion and traversal. Example: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };

questions.question: An integer array starts at address 2000; each integer occupies four bytes. Find address of arr[5].
questions.answer: Assume normal C zero-based indexing and base=&arr[0]=2000. Address(arr[5])=2000+5×4=2020. If base were arr[1] the answer would differ, but C convention is zero-based.

questions.question: Explain priority queue and its significance.
questions.answer: A priority queue removes the highest-priority (or lowest-key) element first, not simply the earliest arrival. Typical binary heap gives O(log n) insert/extract and O(1) peek. Applications: OS job scheduling, Dijkstra's algorithm, event simulation, emergency triage and best-first search.

questions.question: Stack operations PUSH(10), PUSH(20), POP, PUSH(10), PUSH(20), POP, POP, POP, PUSH(20), POP: list popped values.
questions.answer: Stack states (bottom→top): [10], [10,20], POP→20 leaving [10], PUSH10→[10,10], PUSH20→[10,10,20], POP→20, POP→10, POP→10, PUSH20→[20], POP→20. Popped sequence: 20, 20, 10, 10, 20.

questions.question: Illustrate indexed sequential search.
questions.answer: Store sorted data divided into blocks, with an index recording each block's key range or first/maximum key. Search index (binary search possible), then sequentially scan only the selected block. Example records [10,15,18 | 25,27,29 | 40,45] and index of block maximums [18,29,45]: search 27 → block 2 → scan 25,27. Index overhead trades extra memory for faster search.

questions.question: Explain nonlinear data structures with an example.
questions.answer: In a nonlinear structure, relationships are not a single predecessor/successor chain; a node may connect to several others. A tree has hierarchical parent/child links (e.g. binary search tree); a graph allows arbitrary vertices and edges (e.g. road network). Typical operations: tree traversal DFS/BFS and graph connectivity or shortest paths.

questions.question: Significance of threaded binary trees.
questions.answer: A threaded binary tree replaces otherwise null left/right child pointers with inorder predecessor/successor links, marked by tag bits to distinguish threads from children. It enables efficient inorder traversal without recursion or an explicit stack and uses unused pointer slots. Insertion/deletion must maintain thread consistency.

questions.question: Row-major array ARR[-5..15,10..20], element size 2, base address 2500. Find address of ARR[10][15].
questions.answer: Number of columns N2=20−10+1=11. Row-major offset in elements = (i−L1)×N2+(j−L2)=(10−(−5))×11+(15−10)=15×11+5=170. Byte offset=170×2=340. Address=2500+340=2840.

questions.question: Illustrate a stack implemented using singly linked list, with PUSH/POP.
questions.answer: Representation: TOP→[30|next]→[20|next]→[10|null]. PUSH(x): allocate node n; n.data=x; n.next=top; top=n. POP(): if top==NULL report underflow; else x=top->data; old=top; top=top->next; free(old); return x. Both operations O(1) time; space O(n). No fixed capacity except available memory.

questions.question: Construct binary tree from inorder B C A E G D H F I J and preorder A B C D E G F H I J.
questions.answer:
Use first preorder element as root and split inorder at that element, recursively.
Result:
A
├─L: B
│   └─R: C
└─R: D
    ├─L: E
    │   └─R: G
    └─R: F
        ├─L: H
        └─R: I
            └─R: J
Verify: inorder B,C,A,E,G,D,H,F,I,J and preorder A,B,C,D,E,G,F,H,I,J match the paper.

questions.question: Construct AVL tree by inserting 71,41,91,56,60,30,40,80,50,55.
questions.answer:
One correct final AVL tree after standard rotations:
56
├─L: 40
│  ├─L: 30
│  └─R: 50
│     ├─L: 41
│     └─R: 55
└─R: 71
   ├─L: 60
   └─R: 91
      └─L: 80
Key rotations include LR at 71 after insertion 60; LL at 71 after insertion 30; LR at 41 after insertion 40; RL balancing inside the left subtree after inserting 55. For every node, |height(left)−height(right)| ≤1.
questions.explanation: Tree derived by a separate AVL insertion simulation.

questions.question: Explain DFS algorithm with example and name data structures used for DFS and BFS.
questions.answer: Depth-first search starts at a vertex, marks it visited, and repeatedly visits an unvisited neighbor (recursion or explicit stack). For graph A→B,C; B→D; C→E, one DFS traversal is A,B,D,C,E; actual order depends on adjacency ordering. Algorithm: DFS(u): visited[u]=true; for each v adjacent to u, if not visited[v], DFS(v). DFS uses a stack/recursion; BFS uses a FIFO queue. Both run O(V+E) with adjacency lists.

questions.question: Explain asymptotic notations, time–space tradeoff and abstract data type (ADT).
questions.answer:
Asymptotic notation: O(g(n)) bounds runtime from above up to a constant; Ω(g(n)) bounds it below; Θ(g(n)) provides a tight asymptotic bound. Example insertion into unsorted array can be O(1) at end; binary search on sorted array is Θ(log n), sequential scan worst case Θ(n).
Time–space tradeoff: using extra memory can save time, e.g. a hash table consumes O(n) extra space for expected O(1) lookup versus repeated linear scans O(n).
ADT: a logical interface specifying operations/behavior independently of representation, e.g. Stack ADT supports push, pop, peek and isEmpty; implementations may use arrays or linked nodes.

C program to check whether parentheses are balanced in an expression.
Hash 43,165,62,123,142 into ten buckets with h(key)=key%10 and linear probing. Locate 142.
questions.answer: Buckets indexed 0..9. Insert 43→3; 165→5; 62→2; 123 hashes to 3 (occupied), so placed at 4; 142 hashes to 2 (occupied), probes 3(43),4(123),5(165), and inserts at 6. Final table: index 2:62, 3:43, 4:123, 5:165, 6:142; all others empty. Location of 142 = bucket index 6 (zero-based).

questions.question: Merge-sort 11,16,13,11,4,12,6,7. Give time and space complexity.
questions.answer: Divide into [11,16,13,11] and [4,12,6,7]. Sort halves: [11,11,13,16] and [4,6,7,12]. Merge: [4,6,7,11,11,12,13,16]. Recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n) yields Θ(n log n) time in best/average/worst cases. Standard array merge sort uses Θ(n) auxiliary space and Θ(log n) recursion stack.

questions.question: Build an order-4 B-tree inserting a,g,f,b,k,d,h,m,j,e,s,i,r,x,c,l,n,t,u,p.
questions.answer:
Assume order 4 means at most 4 children / 3 keys per node (2-3-4 B-tree), with standard split-full-before-descent insertion. Final tree:
Root [f | k]
├─ child0 [b]
│  ├─ [a]
│  └─ [c d e]
├─ child1 [h]
│  ├─ [g]
│  └─ [i j]
└─ child2 [m | r | t]
   ├─ [l]
   ├─ [n p]
   ├─ [s]
   └─ [u x]
Every leaf is at the same depth; all nodes have 1–3 keys (except transient splits).
questions.explanation: Computed by top-down order-4 B-tree insertion; other equivalent insertion conventions can yield a structurally different valid tree.

questions.explanation: An inorder traversal of a BST gives keys in nondecreasing order.

questions.question: Compare adjacency matrix and adjacency list representations of a graph.
questions.answer: Adjacency matrix is a V×V array A where A[u][v] records an edge/weight. Space Θ(V²), O(1) adjacency test, and O(V) neighbor scan; good for dense graphs. Adjacency list stores a list of neighbors for each vertex: space Θ(V+E), O(deg(v)) neighbor traversal, slower arbitrary adjacency check unless hashed; good for sparse graphs. For undirected graphs, matrix is symmetric and adjacency-list edges occur in both endpoint lists.

questions.question: Explain graph, weighted graph, vertex degree, connected/disconnected graph, cycle, directed/undirected graph and MST.
questions.answer: Graph G=(V,E) consists of vertices and edges. Weighted graph assigns a cost/length to edges. In an undirected graph, degree(v) counts incident edge ends; in a digraph use indegree and outdegree. Connected undirected graph has a path between every pair of vertices; disconnected has multiple components. A cycle is a closed walk with no repeated internal vertices (in a simple cycle). Directed edges are ordered pairs u→v; undirected edges have no orientation. A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected weighted undirected graph is an acyclic set of V−1 edges connecting every vertex with minimum total edge weight; Kruskal and Prim find an MST.
